speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF LIFTING OF EMBARGO ON SHIPMENT OF ARMS TO SPAIN
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked whether the embargo on arms going into Spain would now be lifted with respect to nationalist Spain.
The answer is that in 1937 action was taken to prohibit the export of arms to Spain, the recruiting of Canadians for service in Spain and the issue of passports to Canadian nationals proposing to go to Spain for the purpose of participating in the conflict. This action was taken in view of the existence of civil war in that country and of the fact that similar action had been taken - by the United Kingdom, the United States and most European countries. As I indicated in this house last year, the purpose of these measures was-
-to prevent Canada from being drawn into foreign conflicts by the actions either of manufacturers of munitions or the organizers of foreign recruiting.

In view of the fact that the civil war in Spain has now ended, and that the whole of Spanish territory is now under the control of a single government, steps are now being taken to rescind the above measures which, as I have indicated, were passed in view of the existence of civil war in that country.

speechtext: The bill has nothing to do directly with water powers. It is entirely an emergency measure to meet unforseen situations which might arise out of such conditions as flooding and the like. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: "ANAPA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION OF SEPTEMBER 15, 1938-EMERGENCY CONTROL BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
Perhaps I
might give the detailed information I have which may answer three or four questions at the same time. The reason for the extensive powers provided for in this bill is that the convention gives to the international joint commission a type of function that is essentially different from those performed under

Rainy Lake Water Levels
the boundary waters treaty. The commission is to devise and carry out emergency control measures. While in point of form it is to deal with low water emergencies, practically speaking, in the great majority of instances its work will be concerned with flood conditions. The problem of coping with flood conditions in international waters requires extensive powers which would need to go to the extent of the actual operation of an international dam in the case of emergency. It is not anticipated that the commission will itself operate the dams, but it must have the legal power and authority to do so to ensure that the companies operating the dams will obey its directions. In most instances there is a serious conflict between the owner of the dam and the ordinary inhabitants. The commission may inevitably be compelled to give orders contrary to the interests of the owners of dams, and it is for this reason that the extensive powers are conferred upon it.
The general scheme of the bill is to extend the powers and procedure under the boundary waters treaty to enable the commission to perform the functions imposed upon it by the convention, and to provide for the aid of the exchequer court, if the necessity arises, to ensure obedience by private interests to the orders of the commission. Expenditures would be made by the private interests and controlled in the same manner as expenditures are controlled under the operations of the international joint commission.

subtopic: "ANAPA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION OF SEPTEMBER 15, 1938-EMERGENCY CONTROL BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
I assume when the Prime
Minister refers to expenditures by private interests, he has reference to expenditures for the erection of dams. My own belief is that the erection of these dams should be carried out by those who are affected mostly by floods. In the past the people most affected have been those who own the water powers. They have suffered serious damage from flooding and they have been very anxious to have something of this kind done. I am just wondering who are the private interests referred to by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: "ANAPA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION OF SEPTEMBER 15, 1938-EMERGENCY CONTROL BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
As I mentioned a moment ago, the international joint commission has control of the entire situation. The commission is in the nature of an arbitration tribunal, and it would direct by whom the expenses should be met. Undoubtedly it would in some cases give directions as to precautions to prevent flooding and would determine in such cases how those particular measures were to be enforced. The text of the convention as a whole appears as a schedule, and I think I can give to my hon. friend in a word or two the essential
feature on which he is anxious to obtain information:
Accepting as a basis of agreement the following recommendations made by the international joint commission in its final report dated May 1, 1934, on the reference concerning Rainy lake and the boundary waters flowing into and from that lake, and particularly in answer to question 2 of that reference namely, that it would be wise and in the public interest that the commission be clothed with power to determine when unusual or extraordinary conditions exist throughout the watershed, whether by reason of high or low water, and that it be empowered to adopt such measures of control as to it may seem proper with respect to existing dams at Kettle falls and International falls, as well as any future dams or works, in the event of the commission determining that such unusual or extraordinary conditions exist. Have resolved to conclude a convention for that purpose and have accordingly named as their plenipotentiaries:
The names are given, and then it goes on:
Who, after having communicated to each other their full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed as follows:
Article 1
The international joint commission, established pursuant to the provisions of the treaty signed at Washington on the 11th day of January, 1909, relating to questions arising between Canada and the United States of America, is hereby clothed with power to determine when emergency conditions exist in the Rainy lake watershed, whether by reason of high or low water, and the commission is hereby empowered to adopt such measures of control as to it may seem proper with respect to existing dams at Kettle falls and International falls, as well as with respect to any existing or future dams or works in boundary waters of the Rainy lake watershed, in the event the commission shall determine that such emergency conditions exist.
As I say, the commission is given the power to determine what is to be done, and in so doing will determine all aspects of expenditure' in relation thereto.

speechtext: The point raised by the last speaker (Mr. Heaps) recalls some experiences that Canada has had in connection with the regulation of the water levels of lake Nipissing. The riparian proprietors claimed that the operation of the dam had caused erosion and flooding and damage to their property, and upon those grounds they made claims upon the dominion government. It is a phase of this question which I think is very important indeed. Where would the responsibility rest for damage of that kind? Claims will certainly be made upon this government, petitions will be presented from time to time, and they will have to be disposed of in some manner. The claims would be perennial, coming up all the time. subtopic: "ANAPA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION OF SEPTEMBER 15, 1938-EMERGENCY CONTROL BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION

ously affected by the action which has been taken. I am sure the government will find that with the best of intentions, claims will develop. How will such claims be disposed of? Where is the ultimate liability with respect to such a claim?

speechtext: Has it been estimated how much money, if any, this country will have to put up to carry out the works proposed under this bill? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: "ANAPA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION OF SEPTEMBER 15, 1938-EMERGENCY CONTROL BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend is wrong when he spoke of this as an international river. It is indeed a large area covered by water which flows in two directions. I know that the member for Winnipeg North is well acquainted with it, as I am myself. It has been subject over a long period to agreement between Manitoba and Ontario and the adjoining states. There are numerous present developments, based on normal water levels and normal amounts of water to be used by each power authority. As I see it, this is merely empowering a body which already exists, namely the international joint commission, to give orders with respect to emergent conditions when they arise. Such orders will be obligatory upon all those who now own the dams which maintain the water levels of that great area. We are not dealing with something new.

subtopic: "ANAPA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION OF SEPTEMBER 15, 1938-EMERGENCY CONTROL BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext: That is what I want to bring out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: "ANAPA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION OF SEPTEMBER 15, 1938-EMERGENCY CONTROL BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
If my memory serves me correctly, all the water power available for that great area is now in process of use. The dams are all there; and as a result of the experience of a number of years it has been found desirable to have some single authority which could give orders to all dam owners
Rainy Lake Water Levels

in cases of crisis either by reason of flood, on the one hand, or of shortage on the other. The international joint commission on which both countries are represented was set up for that purpose, and in connection with the convention which is extending to them these powers, the two provinces concerned have no objection; so that it is really a matter of creating single authority so far as giving orders is concerned. At the present time, as I understand it, something may be done under the authority of the province of Manitoba in connection with the Manitoba portion, and something different may be done, in connection with another dam, by the province of Ontario, all of which would make proper coordination difficult in times of emergent conditions due to flood. As I see it, this is merely a method of providing one authority to whom all those interested may represent conditions as they arise, and which may be able to look at the whole picture, instead of a part of it, as would be the case with Manitoba or Ontario or the state of Minnesota. Really that is all that is involved.

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 39, to amend the Department of Transport Stores Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
71492-167A

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext:
Might we have a
brief explanation of the bill, why it is brought in, and what it is supposed to do?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext:
This bill amends the Department of Transport Stores Act which was passed at the last session. It has been found in practice that the stores act did not, in one or two particulars, accomplish what was intended. It will be remembered that the act gave authority to consolidate the stores of the separate branches, that is, the canals branch, the lighthouse branch, the radio branch, the marine branch and the aviation branch. It also provided that the department could anticipate the appropriations for the fiscal year to the extent of 81,000,000. The reason for that provision is that, at the beginning of the fiscal year, it is necessary to move large quantities of supplies to lighthouses and to undertake certain works having to do with the opening of navigation. The provision intended that expenditures up to $1,000,000 could be made from the appropriations of the next fiscal year, but the auditor general has interpreted the word "appropriations" as meaning money that has been voted by parliament. That is, in spite of the intent of the act, the auditor general has not permitted the de-. partment to use funds in advance of those actually being voted by the house. The amount of such purchases is still limited to a maximum of $1,000,000, but this allows us to anticipate appropriations to that extent in order to facilitate the work of the department.
The other change is in connection with the maximum amount of stores allowed to be in stock at the end of the fiscal year. The act now provides that the amount of stores should not be in excess of the amount held by the department at the end of the preceding fiscal year, which amount is about $850,000. On examining the work of the department, and having in mind the extension of the aviation branch, it has ueen determined that the maximum amount of stores at the end of a fiscal year should be fixed at not more than $1,250,000 instead of as provided under the' act as it now stands. Those are the only changes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext:
In other words, it
enables the department to spend money before it has been definitely appropriated by parliament?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext:
To order current supplies,
such as food for lighthouses and such materials as may be required in connection
Transport Stores Act

with the opening of canals. Unfortunately, the opening of the navigation season usually precedes the passage of the estimates by this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext:
I understand the
difficulty. Is there any precedent for this in any other act of this parliament?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext: There are several departments that have revolving funds of that kind. For instance, the national harbours board is entitled to expend $1,000,000 beyond its appropriation, with the understanding that this amount will be the first charge on the new appropriations. The printing bureau also has provision for a revolving fund, and I believe last year the Department of Mines and Resources set up a revolving fund for work among the Indians.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext: I am not raising any objection; I am merely seeking information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext: Broadly speaking, there is a principle running through acts relating to several departments, that where stores are obviously required to be maintained in order that current operations may be continued, there is a provision either of this sort or of the kind that exists in connection with the printing bureau, so that continuity of operation may be possible. In each instance there is a limitation placed by parliament on the amount of stores that may be in stock at any time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext: Will this entirely meet the provisions of the Audit Act and the authority of the comptroller of the treasury, without any specific reference to that point?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY

This amendment has been
suggested by the auditor general, who agrees with us as to the intent of the act passed last year but who has raised the technical difficulty that makes the present act inoperative. It was intended that we could anticipate the passing of the estimates to the extent of $1,000,000, but the auditor general raised the technical point that an estimate does not become an appropriation until it has been approved by the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext: Under the old act would it be necessary to get the authority of the comptroller of the treasury before any expenditure could be made?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING OUTSTANDING ADVANCES AND INVENTORY
speechtext: Quite, but this amendment is our authority for anticipating our vote. In other words, with this authority in hand there will be no difficulty about getting the approval of the comptroller of the treasury.

Section agreed to.

On section 2-Inventory.

speechtext:
Some weeks ago I asked
for a return of correspondence dealing with the situation in Australia, and the return was brought down yesterday. I should like to refer both the Minister of Trade and Commerce ' (Mr. Euler) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) to the documents in this return. The first letter to which I should like to refer is dated September 15, 1938, from the Canadian trade commissioner in Sydney, Australia, to Mr. Wilgress in
Ottawa. This letter deals with salmon being sold under the Japanese label, and points out:
I am sending you concurrently one tin, 3J oz. size, of beauty brand fancy pink salmon, which bears on the label
"Packed for Tonson Packing Company,
Sydney, N.S.W. packed in Japan"
However, the top of the container bears the letters CAN, as shown in the attached pressing.
I brought this to the attention of the chief inspector of the department of health for New South Wales, and he purchased several cans from Seifridges Limited (no connection with Selfridges of London), so that he might consider whether or not this was calculated to deceive a purchaser who might think that the marking on the can meant "Canada." He is not of the opinion at the moment that any definite action on his part would be warranted; nevertheless he is keeping this occurrence under observation and will probably have an opportunity of bringing the matter to the attention of such organizations as the housewives' association.
The whole subject of labelling and competition from Japan in the canned salmon trade is the cause of much concern at the present time, and I am now bringing this matter to your attention so that you may advise the Department of Fisheries respecting our efforts to deal with such instances as the present one. For this purpose I am attaching an additional copy of this letter, and I assume that you will hand the can of salmon to the Department of Fisheries after you have had an opportunity of examining it.
Then there is a cable dated January 11, 1939, from Mr. Cosgrave in Australia, which reads as follows:
Referring to my letter of 15th September canned salmon marking embossed lettering CAN referred regarded as contravention of commerce trade description act. Though shipments in transit 30th November will be admitted strict compliance necessary further shipments by indelible marking produce of union of socialist soviet republics in Asia in conjunction with lettering CAN. Suggest that you advise department fisheries and Vancouver, B.C., Canada.
Then, apparently without the Minister of Fisheries knowing anything about it, Australia took steps to help us out. There is also a letter to Mr. Wilgress from Mr. Bryan in Liverpool, dated February 22, 1939, with regard to Japanese salmon. This points out that the same thing is happening in Great Britain, and states:
Under separate cover I am sending you a sample tin of Siberian medium red salmon, which I picked up when interviewing the trade yesterday and which may be a direct infringement of the Canadian trade mark.
You will note that the top of this tin is embossed with the word CAN in a circle and I understand that quite large quantities of this particular tin reached this market last year.
Messrs. Jos. Travers and Son, 44, Stanley street, Liverpool, from whom I procured this sample, received a considerable quantity of it. They explained that, in connection with a shipment of Siberian medium red salmon sold to
Meat and Canned Foods Act

a Bristol firm, they received a reply from the buyer stating that, while his order called for Siberian medium red, he was glad to see they had sent him Canadian salmon at the same price.
This proves conclusively that, even though this particular embossing is not intended to be an imitation of the Canadian tin, it is having this effect, and I think that action should be taken officially to put a stop to it, as I do not believe for a moment that the British government would tolerate unfair business practices of this kind.
It may be an attempt on the part of the Japanese shippers to participate in the increased demand and call for Canadian salmon as a result of our publicity during the last couple of years.
In other words, the Japanese are trying to cash in on our "Canada calling" campaign in Great Britain. The letter goes on:
I shall be glad to learn what action is taken to counteract the use of this salmon tin on the British market.
That was 'six weeks ago. Has any action been taken by either the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of National Revenue?

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Vancouver South, when he was drawing up his request for correspondence, so drew it that it was confined to communications passing between the government and officials in Australia. He did not extend it to correspondence with officials in Canada. I had an opportunity of glancing at the file to-day, and I see that what correspondence there was, referred to, indeed announced, that in the early spring there was going to be a meeting of the canned salmon producers of British Columbia with the officials.
fMr. Green.]
No date was mentioned, but it was indicated that the meeting would be in January or February, perhaps. I should like the Minister of Fisheries to say if the department is ever going to deal with this subject and discuss what could be done to meet the situation, perhaps by greater care on the part of the companies in putting up and marketing their product; and what the government will do to offset this very obvious attempt to palm off Japanese salmon or salmon caught in Siberian waters as our Canadian salmon. Putting the letters CAN on top of the can to give the impression that it is a Canadian product is thoroughly in line with what the Japanese have done in other lines of trade. They have in Japan a town called U.S.A. and another called Chicago, and they can mark their goods "Made in U.S.A.", but the fact that it is U.S.A. in Japan does not appear obvious to the ordinary housewife.
I call attention to something similar which I took up a year ago but did not get very far with it; in fact, I did not get anywhere. I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Fisheries would combine with the Minister of National Revenue to do something about this matter. It was discovered that when Australia gave us a preference on our salmon, the Japanese trade immediately took steps to offset that. It appears that there was a broker of great prominence and influence who was in the habit of handling Japanese goods exclusively, and he did not like to see the Japanese trade slip away. So he devised this scheme, and it has not even been denied. They sent over to Japan and got labels printed there, because cheap labour in [DOT] Japan made it cheaper to get the labels printed there than in Vancouver. The labels had on them, "Printed in Japan." Then they sent them over, not to the manufacturer because in that case the Minister of National Revenue could have got after them, but to the broker in Vancouver, and he put them on our Canadian goods and shipped them over to Japan. Then he got payments of drawbacks, because these labels were brought into Canada, and in a certain sense were used in our own remanufacture, and so were entitled to drawback. The Minister of National Revenue said flatly that he could not see any way in which he could reject their claim for drawback of duty on those labels brought in under conditions of cheap labour in Japan and used to give a black eye to our Canadian producers and steal the trade away from them. If the article to be shipped over was good, as it would be having been inspected by us, and it gave the impression it

Meat and Canned Foods Act
was put up by Japan, with Japanese labels, that was all to the good of Japanese trade. But if Australia had the same idea that other people have, of not wanting to buy Japanese goods, then they would unknowingly be rejecting our Canadian goods. I took the matter up very thoroughly a year ago. Now I see on the order paper a question respecting some man called Earle Page, an Australian official of some kind.

Can the minister tell me if Mr. Page did come here, and whether he met with the Minister of National Revenue or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and whether any steps will be taken in this matter? It is unthinkable that we should allow this thing to go on by which our Canadian goods, which we spend so much to advertise, should go to Australia, a friendly country, marked made or put up by Japan, and that we should allow into this country cheap labels, produced under cheap labour conditions, and give them a drawback under the conditions I have indicated. Some way should be found within the scope of the rules of the Department of National Revenue whereby this matter could be dealt with, and if there is no other way, at least refuse the drawback. Not only are they using these cheap labels, but they are palming off their salmon as ours.

I have now had an opportunity to look further into this return, and I find that following the letter from Mr. Bryan to Mr. Wilgress, Mr. Fortington, chief of the commodity division, wrote to Mr. Cowie, acting deputy minister of fisheries, on March 7 of this year, as follows:
Japanese Salmon in Britain
Attached is a duplicate of a letter dated the 22nd ultimo received from our office in Liverpool and under separate cover we are forwarding the sample to which reference is made.
If conditions are as they seem to be, this question would seem to warrant special attention. In any event, we shall much appreciate your continued cooperation by advising us as to the nature of the reply which should be sent to the Canadian trade commissioner in Liverpool.
Mr. Cowie, acting deputy minister of fisheries, replied on March 11 as follows:
I have your letter of March 7 with which was enclosed one to you from your trade commissioner in Liverpool, England, with regard to what appears to be misrepresentation in marking a quarter tin of Siberian salmon, a sample tin of which was received with your letter.
I have no doubt in my mind that the letters CAN embossed on the tin sent by your trade commissioner are intended to give buyers the impression that they have been supplied with a tin of Canadian salmon, particularly when they know that our regulations call for the embossing of the word "Canada" on tins of Canadian salmon. To be sure, the mark on the Siberian tin is an abbreviation, but I do think that no one could be persuaded into thinking that it was not meant to convey the idea that it was a tin of Canadian salmon.
I would suggest as the simplest way of dealing with this matter that your trade commissioner at Liverpool be instructed to lay the subject matter before the proper authorities in Great Britain and state that this department feels that the mark referred to on the Siberian tin is one that is bound to mislead consumers into thinking they are buying Canadian salmon.
Has anything been done to follow up that suggestion?

(d)	the name and address of the person, firm or corporation by whom they are packed or by whom they are imported.
It is plain that the law foflbids any importer to import Japanese canned fish unless the label on the can indicates clearly that they come from Japan, what are the contents, and the name and address of the person who imports them. As section 26 of the act now stands, it says that " all cans of fish or shellfish imported " shall be labelled, and paragraph (d) refers to the place where they are packed, and by -whom: the word used is " they," which evidently refers to cans. But suppose that fish is imported from Japan, and after the cans arrive here the importer takes the contents out of the can and puts that same fish into his own cans, bearing Canadian labels; I do not think there is, anything in this section to prohibit that.
Mr. STIRLING; Does he ever do it?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES

speechtext:
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 60, to amend the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act, 1935.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Governor in council upon advice of commission may prescribe standards and establish grades.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Will the minister explain this bill a little more fully?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
I cannot give a great deal more explanation than is given in the explanatory note, except what I said on the introduction of the resolution. The Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act is now under the administration of the tariff board, as my hon. friend probably knows. The late Hon. G. H. Sedgewick, chairman of the board, came to me some weeks ago and recommended an amendment to the act which would enable the commission to establish standards for various commodities-those standards being really fixed I think in collaboration or cooperation with the national research council

 and also giving the board power to prescribe the words under which any commodity may be described. For example, in the matter of textiles, certain manufacturers have marked their products as being wool or silk when as a matter of fact there was a very small proportion of wool or silk in them. In his opinion there was a good deal of misrepresentation. He thought it would be well that the commission be given power to establish standards and descriptions of the various commodities. That is practically all the bill means. It is an amendment to an act which was passed at the instance of the former government, and a good many clauses of

Trade and Industry Commission
which were declared ultra vires, as my hon. friend knows. This is one correction that the chairman of the tariff board thought it well to make, and I have taken his advice in presenting the bill.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Does this bill make it compulsory for people to mark the quality of the goods they sell?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: That would come under the regulations, would it not?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Anyone can make complaint in regard to any commodity along the lines suggested, and if the commission then decides so to recommend to the government, those dealing in the goods would be compelled to mark them in the manner prescribed, or to maintain certain standards. Then it becomes a matter of law and must be observed, in precisely the same way, I think, as is provided for in the Food and Drugs Act, the Meat and Canned Foods Act, and the grain act. In those acts certain standards are set up to which the manufacturers must conform, for the protection of the general public and the consumer.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Would it be possible in this bill to deal with some of the practices referred to in discussing the former bill?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: I understand they apply only to Canadian goods sold in other countries. This bill, I think, would refer to goods sold in Canada and which might also of course be exported.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Will this bill apply to all commodities?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
I notice in the explanatory note, the fourth line from the last, the statement "some cases seem urgent." Then it refers to the knitters of hosiery having made out a strong case for the desirability of rules

covering the marking of the fibre content of hosiery and desiring immediate action. This is a matter on which possibly the hon. member for the Yukon (Mrs. Black) could speak with more authority than I, but I am informed by people who buy and use ladies' hosiery that there seems to be something approaching a "racket"-I do not like the word-in the manufacture of ladies' hosiery; that the quality is extremely low or bad. I should like to know if this bill would apply to a case of that kind, whether the manufacturers of such goods would be compelled to produce some better quality than they do now.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: The commission, of course, cannot dictate what the quality shall be, but they can say that the description must be correct. The article to which my hon. friend refers is, I believe, one of those that the commission wants to deal with. Let us take hosiery, for instance. I merely spoke of textiles, being a very modest man, but if the hosiery were marked "silk" they must contain a certain fixed proportion of silk; if they were wool that would have to be shown; if they were silk and wool that would have to be shown; if they were silk and cotton that would have to be shown, perhaps even with the proportions given. That rests within the powers of the commission. The whole purpose of the bill is to protect, the public so that goods may not be offered as something they are not.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
In the case of women's
hosiery the more expensive qualities are always marked, but if you get a less expensive silk stocking you are likely to have a run. I am not sure that the minister would know what a run is-

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: I think I would; I am a married man.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: -except during an election. I thoroughly agree that all these articles should be marked, regardless of what the price may be.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
I should like to say a word in behalf of the ladies, in support of the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for the Yukon. The ladies have a great deal of difficulty and complain a great deal in regard to the wearing qualities of the hose manufactured and sold to-day. It must be annoying, as well as very hard on the pocketbook, to find a run in a silk stocking the first time it is worn, because after that it is totally useless. I do not know whether this discussion properly comes under this bill, but it does seem to me that some department should inquire into the question whether or

Trade and Industry Commission
not there is any deliberate effort or agreement on the part of manufacturers to refrain from producing and marketing stockings which will not run. I understand that there is a weave that is run-proof, but I believe these stockings are not readily available in our stores; the tendency is to sell stockings that will run, in order that sales may be increased. This matter should be looked into by some department of the government, in order that we may know just what is happening with regard to the production of silk stockings.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that the marking provision of this bill will apply only to goods for export?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: No, indeed not.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
To domestic and export
goods as well?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
I suppose it will really cover all goods manufactured in this country, but the immediate purpose of the legislation as far as I know is to protect the Canadian consumer of these goods. In fact as far as stockings and textiles are concerned this step is taken following an investigation which was made in response to a request by the garment manufacturers' association, who complained that lines of goods were coming on the market marked in such a way as to be not representative of the actual content of the commodity, and that trade was thereby being injured.
With regard to what the hon. member for Wellington South has said, I hardly think the government can interfere and tell manufacturers that they must produce a runless stocking, or anything of that sort. I should think if they could produce such a commodity they should advertise, telling the people how good their commodity is, and thus sell more stockings. As a matter of fact I never heard that there was such a thing as a runless stocking.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: There is a runless stocking; instead of a run you get a little pin prick of a hole, and I would rather have the run.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member for Yukon or the hon. member for Wellington South could tell us the name of this runless stocking; I have a daughter.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
Perhaps I should not ask this question, but I see these words:
-prescribe the manner in which such commodity shall be sold, offered for sale, or displayed for sale.
So far the discussion has been in connection with textiles. Can any other commodity be discussed, or does this deal with textiles only?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Paint is another commodity in connection with which I believe they want to take some action. One could imagine almost any number of commodities that might be concerned; my hon. friend can imagine them as well as I can.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: I am quite in accord with any article being thoroughly marked, as is provided by this section. One article I have in mind is the ordinary wrench. I am told by manufacturers of wrenches in this country that at the moment considerable quantities of these tools are coming from Germany. They are not marked in any way but are being imported in a roundabout manner through the United States. I am heartily in support of this section if it means that every item coming into this country, of a size which would permit it to be designated as to country of manufacture, should be so designated, whether it is made in Germany, France, or anywhere else.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: I should not like there to be any misunderstanding with regard to the matter referred to by my hon. friend. If it is desired that goods coming from other countries should be marked, that would come under the Department of National Revenue. If the minister of that department brings in a recommendation to council that a certain commodity, wrenches, if you like, shall be marked with the name of the country of origin, once council adopts that recommendation it becomes law. This has nothing to do with that, however; this has to do with the fixing of standards of commodities manufactured in this country and the marking of the names by which they shall be designated.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Will this control the marking of goods such as socks, which are often sold as all wool when in reality they are made from shoddy?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Exactly that sort of thing.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: Since we are delegating a great deal of power to the commission, I should like to ask the minister why under the penalty clause an individual can ibe thrown into gaol while a corporation cannot. It will be seen that a large corporation, through its manager, can be fined, while an individual may have to pay a fine and go to gaol as well.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext:
The penalty provided for a corporation is a fine not exceeding $5,000, while it is not more than $1,000 in the case of an individual, so apparently some consideration is shown the individual in that way. I suppose the reason you cannot provide a gaol sentence for a corporation is that you
Pension Act Amendments

cannot throw all the members of a corporation, the president, directors and so on, into gaol. The 'bill was drawn up by a distinguished jurist, the late Judge Sedgewick; therefore I take it that it was properly framed.

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: I was wondering how this squares with the provincial power over trade and industry. Does it infringe upon that power?

subtopic: GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL UPON ADVICE OF COMMISSION MAY PRESCRIBE STANDARDS AND ESTABLISH GRADES
speechtext: I would say not; I should think Judge Sedgewick would have been familiar with that point, and of course all bills must pass the Department of Justice.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I suggest if
there is no objection we might take the Canadian National Railway Company securities resolution, and advance it a stage.
Mr. DUNNING moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to issue securities not exceeding $25,821,707 in principal amount to provide the moneys necessary to meet capital expenditures made or to be made during the calendar year 1939 and to make provision for the retirement of capital indebtedness during the said calendar year; to authorize the governor in council to guarantee the principal, interest and sinking funds of such securities; and to authorize the making of temporary loans to the said company secured by such securities and not exceeding $25,821,707 in principal amount to enable the said company to meet such expenditures and indebtedness.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
The object of the bill
which will be based upon this resolution is to provide for the usual Canadian- National financing. It will have to do wholly with capital expenditures as authorized by this house and with making provision for the refunding of maturing indebtednes. It will be exactly the same kind of bill as has been passed by the house during the last number of years. The only advantage in passing the resolution at this time is that it will make the bill available to hon. members in its printed form when they return after the Easter vacation. There will be ample opportunity to discuss any feature of it on the second reading.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Could the minister give
the details that go to make up this amount of capital expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I have not before me
at the moment the amount which will be involved for refunding and the amount which will be involved for capital expenditures. I shall be ready with that information at the next stage of the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Is the Montreal
terminal included in this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Any capital expenditure
on the Montreal terminal will be part of this, but that again is in the railway budget.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Dunning thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 85, respecting Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee Act, 1939.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, as amended by chapter 20 of the statutes of 1935 and by chapter 47 of the statutes of 1938, to provide that proposals for a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement made by farmers under the said act as amended may be received in the province of Manitoba after June 30, 1939.
' Mr. MacINNIS:	I think a brief explanation of this resolution would be in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939
speechtext:
I intended to give the
explanation when we were in committee, but it can be given now just' as well.
It will be remembered that a year ago this house agreed on certain amendments to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, among the most important of which was an amendment which gave power to the government to terminate the operation of that act in any province. It will be remembered that the Senate did not agree with the House of Commons on the amendments, and the bill as it was returned from the Senate was amended bringing to a close the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in all provinces except Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. In the case of Manitoba the Senate made the terminating date June 30, 1939. and in the case of Saskatchewan and Alberta the date was left open. During the year, particularly recently, the government has received representations from Manitoba, not-
Gold Clause Obligations

ably from the legislature, I believe by unanimous resolution, requesting that in view of the conditions prevailing in the province as the result of last year's crop, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act should be continued in Manitoba on the same basis as it is being continued in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The object of the bill to be founded on this resolution is to comply with this request. It will be remembered that a year ago the Commons and Senate disagreed, and, following the procedure provided for such cases, it was necessary to hold a conference. I doubt very much whether the result of that conference was wholly satisfactory to the House of Commons, but an agreement was reached on the legislation. We are now proposing to make an effort to put Manitoba in the same position as Saskatchewan and Alberta because of the parallel conditions which exist.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939
speechtext:
Has it expired in British
Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939
speechtext:
I made an error there.
The Senate amendment provided a termination in June next of the provisions of the act as far as British Columbia is concerned.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939
speechtext:
Will this bill have any
effect whatever on the operations of the act outside of Manitoba, by inference or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939
speechtext: No effect whatever.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939
speechtext: It will be limited entirely to Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ARRANGEMENT ACT AS TO PROPOSALS FOR COMPOSITION, ETC., IN MANITOBA AFTER JUNE 30, 1939
speechtext:
Yes.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Dunning thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 86, to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISCHARGE BY PAYMENT OF NOMINAL OR FACE AMOUNT

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to repeal the Gold Clauses Act 1937, and to provide that obligations payable in gold or gold coin or in an amount of money measured thereby may be discharged by payment of the nominal or face amount thereof.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISCHARGE BY PAYMENT OF NOMINAL OR FACE AMOUNT
speechtext: The object of the bill to be based on this resolution is to accomplish what we thought we had accomplished by the Gold Clauses Act of 1937. Since that act was passed, there have been decisions of the privy council which have clarified the position materially. We desire that there shall be no doubt as to what was intended by the legislation of 1937. That is to say, that obligations payable in gold or in gold coin, or in an amount of money measured by that, may be discharged by the payment of the nominal or face amount of the obligation. I can deal with the matter more fully and with the legal technicalities on the second reading of the bill. The object is to do simply what we intended to do in 1937. It is not a change of policy or a change of intention in any way. It is just that decisions which have been rendered by the highest court in the commonwealth make it necessary for us to change the act in order to carry out our intention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISCHARGE BY PAYMENT OF NOMINAL OR FACE AMOUNT
speechtext: Would the minister explain a little more fully the decision and its effect? What was wrong with the existing legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISCHARGE BY PAYMENT OF NOMINAL OR FACE AMOUNT
speechtext:
It is highly technical,
and I frankly confess that I have not my material before me to-day. I do not desire to press the resolution on the house to-day if there is doubt in anyone's mind regarding it. I shall be fully armed on the second reading. I admit that I should have had the information here, but I doubt if I would fully understand all its implications myself. On the second reading, however, I can convey to the house what the lords of the privy council had to say.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISCHARGE BY PAYMENT OF NOMINAL OR FACE AMOUNT
speechtext:
Very well.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Dunning thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 87, to repeal the Gold Clauses Act, 1937.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES

speechtext:
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories, (a) by grants in aid of the construction, reconstruction and equipment of factories; (b) by grants in aid of insulating

Dairying Industry-Cheese
and refrigerating factory buildings and the purchase of certain equipment; (c) by grants for high grade cheese, out of moneys appropriated by parliament.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
The bill to be based on this resolution purports to do three things. In the first place it provides for grants to cheese factories for the purpose of improving their equipment. We are given to understand that exception is taken at the present time, particularly in the British market, not particularly to the quality or standard of our cheese, but to its form. I am told that in Britain they very much prefer the form of cheese which they make there, which is of a higher type and not so broad as the type of cheese we are turning out in Canada. In order to encourage changing from our forms to the form they desire in Britain, we are proposing to pay half the cost of making the change. That will not involve a very considerable amount of money, probably twenty to thirty thousand dollars all told.
The second proposal in the bill is in connection with the factories and is that where two or more factories or organizations that have a complete factory get together and agree to construct one factory in place of those now operating, in order to lower the costs of production over a certain area and to put in equipment which is more up to date and more in conformity with that used in some of the countries that are competing with us, the government is prepared to assist in the cost of making the change in that particular locality.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Up to what per cent?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Up to fifty per cent but not more.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Fifty per cent of the cost of the general improvements?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
No; fifty per cent of the cost of the materials entering into the reconstruction.
The third proposal in the bill is that we pay a premium of two cents on the higher grade of cheese for the purpose of encouraging the production of a higher standard of cheese.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: May I ask the minister if that two cent bonus will be paid on export cheese only or on all cheese?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
The two cents will be paid on all cheese of the top grade, but top grade only.
Motion agreed to and the house went into
committee. Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: When the minister was making his explanation before we went into committee, he said that the cost of making changes in connection with presses to make the new forms for cheese would amount to $30,000. That means, I assume, that the whole expenditure would amount to that sum.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: It is estimated that the outside cost would be, over the whole area, $30,000 or $10,000.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: All over Canada?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Yes, for that purpose. It is just a matter of changing the rings and forms.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Could the minister give us an idea of the cost of a single installation of these new presses, say in a factory with an output of sixty or seventy tons a year?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Just at the moment I could not give that information, but I will see that it is brought down before the 'bill is considered. .

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: There is another question. The resolution states that there should be grants in aid of not only the improvement of cheese factories, but also the construction and reconstruction of refrigerators, insulation and so-on. Would the minister state whether those factories will have to build according to specifications approved Iby the federal department, and will all necessary equipment have to be installed according to specifications? If so, where will the specifications come from and how are they to be laid down? Could the minister give us some information generally with regard to these matters?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Section 3 of the bill, which I have before me, provides that the governor in council may grant, out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose, a sum not exceeding fifty per centum of the amount actually expended for new material, new equipment and labour utilized in constructing, reconstructing and equipping those cheese factories which are eligible for a subsidy under this act or the regulations. Section 7 provides that the governor in council may make regulations, and these regulations will cover the points that have been raised.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Does the bill refer only to factories now in operation?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Yes, only the replacement of factories now in operation or the putting in of curing rooms in factories now in operation.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
Will the amalgamating of these factories be left to the option of the
Dairying Industry-Cheese

owners of the factories, or will any pressure be brought to bear by the government to have them do this?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: I do not assume that any pressure will be brought to bear by the government. Of course the government would give some assistance in an advisory capacity and would lay down regulations as to what the nature of the construction would have to be in order to come within the terms of the legislation.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: In regard to factories in eastern Ontario, with which I am most familiar, the great difficulty with regard to amalgamation is that our dairies are small. As a rule our farmers have not more than fifteen, twenty or twenty-five cows, and if the factories are amalgamated they would have to draw their milk for too great distances. If we amalgamate our factories and the areas become too large, the cost of drawing milk will be too great. That is the great difficulty in eastern Ontario, and that is why I ask if it will be left to the discretion of the owners of these factories to decide whether amalgamation would be convenient or whether it would pay them to join the factories together.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: It will be left entirely to their discretion as to whether that should be done. This is simply a means of persuading them to do it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Exactly.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
It seems
difficult to arrive at an estimate of twenty or thirty thousand dollars with relation to the whole dominion.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: The hon. member means that he does not think that sum would cover the cost? Oh, no, thirty or forty thousand dollars would not cover all we are talking about; it would cover simply the changing of the rings for the forms for making the cheese, and that part of the equipment. The whole amount required for all we are talking about is estimated at about a quarter of a million dollars.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
This seems an extraordinary bill to add to the bonus- the opportunitjr for any and all cheese factories to start and remodel their plants, and almost to tear them down if they wish to rebuild them, with the government paying for the labour. I assume from the clause which the minister has read that it leaves a latitude wide enough to pay for all sorts of work so far as reconstruction of the cheese factories is concerned. I hope the minister has made some provision that the two cent bonus will be
(Mr. Thompson.]
returned to the farmer and to the producer, if the cheese factory owners are to have an opportunity to remodel their plants in many instances where they are more or less obsolescent. I agree with the principle behind subsidies and bonuses for high-grade export products, but I have my doubts as to the effect of the wide and more or less reckless and haphazard policy which is being brought down at the present time. In one bill it not only gives us a two cent bonus, but allows every cheese factory in Canada to rebuild itself and receive from the dominion treasury dollar for dollar expended.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
I might explain the
matter in this way. The safeguard is the one mentioned by the hon. member for Lanark, that it is available only to cheese factories where there is amalgamation, and these amalgamations would come in only very few instances.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
The clause does not
say so.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: The clause which the minister read did not mention that it was confined to amalgamations.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: Oh, yes, it says that there must be two or more of them amalgamated before the provision applies.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
Even so,
I think it is a very wide and sweeping bill. It seems to me that it benefits the cheese manufacturer more than it does the cheese industry at large. The whole principle of bonuses as suggested by the minister's recent references tends, perhaps, to cover a larger area and serve a smaller national purpose so far as getting high-class export products on the market, and I believe it will cost the treasury of this dominion colossal sums and will not serve the purpose which is intended.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: But look at the votes it will get.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
I think these matters
will be more properly discussed when we have the bill before the house. If hon. members will allow the resolution to go forward, the matter can be discussed fully at that time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext: I do not want to delay the matter at all, but this is a very important bill; we have not had much chance to make a study of it, and I think that the minister might agree to, let the resolution stand.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
If I may be permitted to make Pie suggestion, I believe it will be much easier to study the bill if the committee will permit the legislation to go past the

Criminal Code
resolution stage. The bill is printed and copies can be had to-morrow morning by any who desire to get them. It can be studied during the recess and hon. members may be prepared to discuss it when they come back.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHEESE AND CHEESE FACTORIES
speechtext:
Very well.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Gardiner thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 88, to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURAGEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to encourage the cooperative marketing of any kind of grain, other than wheat, and of other agricultural products defined in the act, by guaranteeing the initial payment of cooperative associations, as in the act defined, with provision also for the appointment and remuneration of officers, clerks and employees necessary for the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Gardiner thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 89, to assist and encourage cooperative marketing of agricultural products.

subtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURAGEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext: The house might like to have the other resolution, so as to have the other bill.

subtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURAGEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURAGEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
